answer.rationale: Timing is the strongest signal available: the release landed 2h ago and the write-path p99 climb started ~90m ago, which puts the change squarely upstream of onset. Rollback is also the only candidate that attacks a suspected cause rather than redistributing symptoms, and it is the least hostile to the primary objective of not losing customer writes. I verify memory_b1 because it is the single memory my action leans on hardest, and its summary is thin in exactly the ways that matter here: it does not say whether that rollback happened under heavy write load, whether the prior build was schema/format-compatible with in-flight data, or how long the drain took. If the archived record shows that rollback was done in a low-traffic window against a compatible build, my confidence rises; if it was a light read-path revert, the analogy to peak settlement writes largely collapses. Regional failover (memory_b2) is the tempting alternative because the degradation is region-confined, but that confinement is equally consistent with a region-scoped rollout of the same release, in which case failover carries the defect with it while forcing a write-path cutover during peak settlement \u2014 the highest-risk moment to move writes. add_capacity (memory_b3) worked as pre-provisioned headroom ahead of a known peak, not as a live remedy for a latency climb that began after a deploy; it would likely just mask a defect. route_read_replicas (memory_b5) addresses read contention on the primary, and the symptom here is write-path p99, so the mechanism does not match. enable_circuit_breaker (memory_b4) contained an external partner outage; there is no partner-failure signal, and failing fast on settlement writes at peak is precisely how customer writes get dropped. Two caveats I am holding rather than resolving. First, every inherited memory records an intervention that succeeded \u2014 there is not one failed or neutral outcome in the set. That is a survivorship-shaped record, so it tells me these actions can work but gives me no base rate for how often each one is the wrong call, and I should not read the confident tone of these summaries as evidence of high prior probability. Second, correlation with the deploy is not causation: a 90-minute ramp coinciding with the settlement peak is also consistent with a load-driven saturation that the release merely made marginally worse. That is the specific downstream risk I am flagging \u2014 rolling back at peak could itself shed or stall in-flight settlement writes, and if the release is not the cause I will have spent my one intervention and must wait for the next window. Hence small_guarded_test rather than broad_rollout: stage the rollback across a bounded slice of primary-region write capacity first, per the canary discipline in memory_b6, with an explicit abort if write-error rate or drain latency worsens, then expand within the same window if p99 responds. If the memory_b1 record reveals a compatibility hazard with the prior build under load, I switch to holding position and treat regional failover as the fallback rather than proceeding.
